summary:
Zambia criminalises consensual same-sex conduct and the prohibition is enforced. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under Zambian law falls within the conduct the law reaches. Amnesty International's campaign account of 26 November 2024, 'Madalitso's story', describes a 36-year-old Zambian medical professional who by November 2024 had served three years of a sentence imposed for consensual same-sex acts; his imprisonment removed a trained clinician from a health system already short of staff.

Police are a documented source of risk rather than protection. The US State Department's 2021 country report records police perpetrating violence and verbal and physical harassment on the basis of gender identity and sexual orientation, and prolonged detentions of LGBTQI+ people. Advocacy groups reported that police routinely solicit bribes after arresting LGBTQI+ individuals, with the fines reportedly raised from 500 to 15,000 kwacha, roughly $30 to $900. The 2022 report adds that officers who detain LGBTQI+ people often threaten charges under other laws to extort payment for release.

Forced anal examinations are used for evidence-gathering in same-sex prosecutions. Human Rights Watch's report of 12 July 2016, 'Dignity Debased', documents the practice in at least eight countries including Zambia, where it was less frequent than in Egypt and Tunisia but where prosecutors have introduced medical reports from anal examinations as court evidence, including in a mass trial of about 20 men. Amnesty International described such examinations in a 2014 case as tantamount to torture and scientifically invalid, and the World Health Organization and medical authorities have condemned them; victims describe them as painful, degrading sexual violence.

Official policy offers no protection. The 2022 report found no credible government efforts to rescind discriminatory laws targeting LGBTQI+ persons, and no credible reports of government agents condoning violence. It also records that President Hakainde Hichilema's statement of 30 May 2022 opposing basic LGBTQI+ protections and same-sex marriage produced a spike in public hate speech, threats and assaults. That 2022 statement and its aftermath are the most recent documented instance of violence in this record; no later incident is sourced here.

Public advocacy on LGBTQ matters is effectively barred. The 2021 State Department report concluded that freedom of expression or peaceful assembly on LGBTQI+ matters remained nonexistent. In 1998 Vice President Christon Tembo called for the arrest of people promoting gay rights, and the Registrar of Societies stated he would refuse to register any LGBTQ organisation. In The People v. Paul Kasonkomona (2013), an activist arrested after calling for decriminalisation on a television talk show was cleared: the Magistrate Court and then the High Court held that he had been reasonably exercising his right to freedom of expression and rejected the soliciting, public place and immoral purposes charges, though the government contested the decision.

Documented incidents of societal violence carry dates. In May 2014 residents of Marapodi in Lusaka apprehended two suspected lesbians and demanded their arrest. In January 2015 an openly gay man was attacked by a mob that reportedly included three police officers. Advocacy groups report that LGBTQI+ people face societal violence driven by prevailing prejudice and misperceptions of the law, and most LGBTQ people in Zambia remain closeted for fear of targeting, with lesbians especially vulnerable in the country's patriarchal structure.

Healthcare access is uneven. There are no broad legal protections against discrimination in health care, and the 2021 report records LGBTQI+ persons facing an inability to access healthcare services; as of July 2007 no public or private programmes provided HIV-related counselling to homosexual men, and the government's National AIDS Control Program does not address same-sex relationships. Two narrower instruments run the other way. The Health Professions Council of Zambia's 2014 Code of Ethics bars practitioners from discriminating in patient management on grounds of sexuality, and the Ministry of Health's 2022 Zambia Consolidated HIV Guidelines require facilities to serve all adolescents regardless of sexual orientation or sexual behaviour.

Public attitudes are largely hostile. A 2010 survey found that 2 percent of Zambians regarded homosexuality as morally acceptable, against 11 percent in Uganda. Organised opposition exists in the form of the NGO Zambia Against People with Abnormal Sexual Acts, formed in 1999 to combat homosexuality, and social attitudes are coloured by perceptions that homosexuality is immoral and a form of insanity, reflecting evangelical religious influence and colonial-era attitudes.
tangentialFactors:
The National Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health Policy of 2015 recognises sexual orientation and gender identities as central aspects of being human, one of the few official statements in this record that names gender identity at all.

Section 158(3) of the penal code, amended in 2005, targets children who commit gross indecency with another child of the same sex, in public or private, or who attempt to procure such acts, making them liable to such community service or counselling as the court may determine in the best interests of the child. There is no parallel offence for minors of opposite sex. The provision concerns residents rather than visitors, but it marks the asymmetry in the code.

The internet and the country's digitisation are credited with exposing younger generations to more stories from different walks of life, and those generations are beginning to show slightly more positive, more open-minded attitudes toward LGBTQ peers. The same period produced the 2022 spike in hate speech described in the 2022 country report, so the two tendencies run alongside each other rather than one replacing the other.

The 2013 Kasonkomona acquittal is the only judicial pushback documented in this record, and the government contested it. It establishes a freedom-of-expression reasoning that has not been shown to have been extended to advocacy in practice, where the 2021 report found expression and assembly on LGBTQI+ matters nonexistent.
localsOnly:
Discrimination in employment, housing and education is documented for LGBTQ people in Zambia, alongside the healthcare discrimination noted in the summary.

Most LGBTQ people in Zambia are closeted due to fear of targeting, and lesbians are described as especially vulnerable within the patriarchal structure. Recourse against mob or communal violence is limited; the January 2015 attack documented in this record reportedly involved three police officers among the mob.

Registration of an LGBTQ organisation is refused in principle, a position stated by the Registrar of Societies in 1998 and consistent with the 2021 finding that assembly on these matters does not exist. The NGO Zambia Against People with Abnormal Sexual Acts, formed in 1999 to combat homosexuality, is the documented organised opposition.

The National AIDS Control Program does not address same-sex relationships, and as of July 2007 no public or private programmes provided HIV-related counselling to homosexual men, at a time when adult HIV prevalence was about 17 percent. Societal discrimination in access to health care and to education is documented by the US State Department (2010) and Global Rights/IGLHRC.

Christine Kaseba, wife of then-President Michael Sata, said in 2013 that silence around men who have sex with men should end and that no one should be discriminated against on the basis of sexual orientation. This is an individual statement from 2013, not government policy.
outOfScopeNotes:
No information on trans-specific healthcare, hormone therapy or medication access appears anywhere in the source inventory for Zambia. The health provisions cited are framed around sexual orientation and, in the 2015 adolescent policy, gender identity; none addresses gender-affirming care.

The inventory contains no sourced rules on passport gender markers, visa or border screening, or document inspection as it affects trans travellers entering Zambia. Nothing in these sources should be read as evidence either way on entry screening.

The violence incidents cited (May 2014, January 2015, and the 2022 spike in assaults) are individual documented events with no denominator, period total or rate attached. The inventory provides no trans-specific violence count for Zambia and no general homicide rate to compare one against, so no relative risk figure can be stated.

The 2 percent morally-acceptable figure is a 2010 survey of Zambian attitudes to homosexuality generally, not a current measure of attitudes toward trans people; it is retained only as dated evidence of the attitude environment. The 2022 report's reference to a spike in hate speech, threats and assaults carries no counts or dates beyond the 30 May 2022 statement that preceded it.

Whether the 2013 Kasonkomona reasoning has been cited or relied on in any later Zambian proceeding is unresolved in these sources.
